title: Backtesting and evaluation
summary: Compare resource forecasts with actual use and understand scores and rankings.
text: Rolling backtests Move forecast origins forward through time. Each run uses only history available before that origin, including all additional input metrics. Match windows and horizons to actual operating decisions. Read resource prediction performance Accuracy concerns resources such as CPU, memory, and GPU. Replica counts are derived from resource demand and constraints; distinguish them from actual and Ready replicas. Measure Meaning and use WAPE Total absolute error relative to total absolute actual values over the same window. Peak underestimation The risk of predicting less than actual high-water demand. Resource accuracy and score Read resource performance, completeness, and protection factors together. Scores do not override execution bounds. Actual evaluation Link observations to predictions after their target times arrive. Scores, rankings, and consensus The rankings page shows current performance and historical changes. Rank helps compare candidates; look-ahead decisions combine available forecasts and confidence rather than simply following the top-ranked method. Inspect training and run details for window, version, parameters, duration, and reasons. Recheck performance after configuration changes. Wait for actuals and keep evaluating Future target times do not yet have actual observations; missing evaluations are not zero error. Continue reviewing resource behavior and outcomes as inputs and workload patterns change. Read a module effect report Select a module and time window in forecasting results to review resource error, peak underestimation, scale-up timeliness, excess and missing capacity, reversals, degradation reasons, and algorithm adoption. Insufficient or unmeasurable data is identified rather than treated as zero error. Actual Pod-hours and capacity SLO The execution and capacity section compares observed Ready replicas with replicas required by measured load. It reports actual, needed, excess, and missing Pod-hours and minutes of insufficient capacity. Data gaps are excluded from compared time. Capacity SLO is time without a capacity shortfall divided by compared time. Its default target is 99%, configured with forecast.slo_capacity_target_percent . It is not a latency or error-rate SLO; excess Pod-hours are not proven monetary savings. Values require at least 12 compared moments covering at least half the requested window. Preview configuration changes Open change preview from the effect report to compare saved and proposed settings on the same history. Review shortfall and surplus windows, risk error, replica-hours, changes, and the largest differences. Compare methods and parameters, safety margin, per-Pod capacity, replica bounds, and short-term correction. Preview is read-only: it saves no recommendations, changes no modules, and performs no scaling. It compares forecast-derived replicas without fully replaying cooldowns, steps, look-ahead, or safeguards. Model services use pretrained models rather than background-tuned copies. Interpret results within this scope.

title: Recommendations and look-ahead
summary: Learn how model consensus, lead time, and constraints shape resource advice.
text: Read a recommendation snapshot A snapshot records resource advice, desired replicas, decisive factors, sources, version, and expiry. It explains what to configure and why; execution records show what was actually applied. Allow time for capacity to become ready Scaling only when demand arrives may be too late. Look-ahead decisions account for collection, prediction, control loops, Pod readiness, and node preparation where needed, then evaluate the corresponding future window. Scale-up and scale-down use different perspectives. Reductions require caution across future demand, live load, and readiness rather than reacting to a brief dip. Multi-model consensus Available candidates participate in the look-ahead window. Confidence combines scores with recent tracking error. A configured weighted quantile combines predictions before live load and safeguards settle the decision. Read consensus alongside the final replica count, constraints, and actual use. Without eligible predictions, use schedules, fallback, or unchanged values according to module rules. Resource and replica constraints CPU, memory, throughput, or JVM pressure may be decisive. Replica changes respect minimums, maximums, hard ceilings, steps, and cooldowns. OOM floors and memory peaks provide protection beyond smoothed point forecasts. Configured or estimated per-Pod capacity needs comparison with workload load tests. Advice, writes, and readiness are separate stages A submitted replica change does not mean the new Pods are Ready. Inspect actual replicas, readiness, and subsequent resource behavior. Forecast far enough for capacity to arrive For modules planning replica scaling, the effective horizon accounts for the module horizon, run interval, and readiness lead time. Default lead-time coverage is twice the lead time, capped at 24 hours, with the reason shown in recommendation details. Once enough scale-up outcomes exist, lead time uses measured readiness for that module and allows for recent late arrivals. Candidates that substantially lag recent actuals are excluded from consensus when healthy alternatives exist. Configurable emergency scale-up can cover observed demand above both forecasts and current capacity. This path only scales up and still respects replica ceilings.

title: Admission and scaling
summary: Enable Pod resource advice and replica scaling separately, then review outcomes.
text: Let the Operator adjust replicas Configure the target workload, replica bounds, step limits, and cooldowns. Auto requires authorization at both module and global levels before the Operator applies valid advice. Manage everything on the platform modules: the operator reads them and writes the replicas, and creates no resource of its own in the cluster. A target has exactly one replica owner. One replica owner per target Do not let the Operator, HPA, KEDA, or duplicate scalers write the same workload. Stop the previous controller and release ownership before reviewing the new controller in Observe. Apply resource advice to new Pods Admission reads the latest valid recommendation and adjusts CPU / memory requests and configured limits on new Pods. Unavailable advice should preserve original resources and allow deployment. New recommendations do not immediately change running Pods. Apply settings through creation or rolling updates. Assess and authorize memory-limit reductions separately. Review actual outcomes Inspect scaling and admission details for advice, applied results, and pause or failure reasons. Check current and Ready replicas, workload demand, and resource use to distinguish a submitted change from ready capacity. Did capacity arrive before demand? Open Expansion timeliness from scale-up records to inspect timely rate, late-arrival P90, emergency share, peak-underestimation P90, horizon-to-lead ratio, and decision wait. Each measure includes sample counts and status. Insufficient samples remain pending; suitable settings alone do not establish successful scale-up outcomes. Upward decisions are evaluated against subsequent demand and Ready replicas as timely, late, or demand not arriving. Evaluated readiness and lateness feed later lead times. This outcome assessment covers scale-ups rather than scale-downs. Report actions after an outage The Operator queues reports before sending and replays them in occurrence order after recovery. --report-spool-file persists them to a mounted file. Deployment manifests use emptyDir, surviving container restarts within the same Pod, not necessarily Pod replacement. The queue holds 10,000 records; overflow drops the oldest and increments a counter. Explicitly rejected records are removed so they do not block later reports. This is bounded delivery storage, not indefinite audit retention. Optional action columns include record_id , occurrence and reporting times, decision source, outage state, and Operator identity. The platform deduplicates by record ID and archives late reports by occurrence time. Requests, limit ratios, and OOM floors When configured, limit ratios apply to the final request: a 10 GiB memory request with a 1.2 ratio produces a 12 GiB limit. OOM uplift raises the request floor without repeatedly compounding the limit ratio. Admission calls carry request_uid and operation for attribution and deduplication. Queries without a request UID still return advice but do not create admission records.

title: Safety and fallback
summary: Manage schedules, fallback, bypass, and safeguards for automatic actions.
text: Modes and authorization Observe and Recommend help build an understanding of workload behavior. Admission and automatic scaling require both global authorization and a suitable module mode. Writes are disabled by default. Scheduled overrides Set fixed resources or replicas for defined business windows, including start, end, timezone, priority, and covered fields. Other fields follow their normal policies; normal calculation resumes after the window. Schedules use explicit IANA timezones and storage stays in UTC. The platform defaults to UTC+8 and pages display UTC+8. Never write converted display times back as storage values. Degradation and recovery Each field follows bypass → schedule → eligible model → module fallback → unchanged. Values must remain valid, fresh, and within bounds. OOM floors apply outside bypass. Record reasons for insufficient history, stale inputs, model failure, or missing eligible forecasts. Consecutive healthy cycles are required before recovery to avoid unstable switching. When manual intervention is needed Enable Bypass and record a reason. Disable the corresponding global setting and return to Recommend or Observe. Review snapshots, action records, and actual resources. Fix inputs or policy and compare results before gradually restoring authorization. Stopping future actions does not undo previous changes Bypass and global settings do not restore earlier resource or replica configurations automatically. Consider current service state and action history when restoring them. Configure OOM memory protection separately Modules separate OOM protection from prediction metrics. Configure lookback, memory uplift, and heap pressure, then connect OOM counts, pre-OOM working set, memory limits, and JVM heap metrics. Rules missing their required inputs do not apply, and recommendation details identify the missing inputs. OOM score weighting is disabled by default. When enabled, it penalizes memory scores only where memory was underallocated in the evaluation window; CPU scores are unaffected. Memory floors provide protection while scores compare models. Hold, degrade, and recover during an outage The Operator tracks each module separately. A connection fault does not immediately switch replicas to fallback. Configure timing in system settings; the platform distributes it. The following describes defaults. State Replica behavior Normal Follow platform decisions within module bounds, cooldowns, and steps. Cached Use a decision less than ten minutes old for scale-up only, without retaining urgency. Holding Without valid cache, retain current replicas for five minutes without immediately applying fallback. Degraded After the hold, move toward fallback in steps, only upward, with degradation cooldown between actions. Recovering Follow upward decisions; scale-down requires both two consecutive successful responses and at least five minutes of stable recovery. Configure decision and module cache lifetimes, hold, fallback cooldown, recovery responses, and stability through operator.decision_cache_ttl_seconds , module_cache_ttl_seconds , degrade_hold_seconds , degrade_cooldown_seconds , recover_answers , and recover_stable_seconds , all under the operator. prefix. Expired module configuration also holds replicas. An explicit no-decision answer outranks cached advice. The decision cache is in memory and does not survive restarts. Offline action reports can be persisted separately; see offline reporting .

title: AI assistant and skills
summary: Query platform state, use slash commands, export reports, and explain changes.
text: Open the AI assistant Enable assistant.enabled in system settings and grant the user assistant:chat . The assistant opens from the top-right button in a floating window. Turning off the global switch hides both the entry and the window. Manage connections and skills under AI configuration. Ask which modules need attention, whether a service scaled in time, or what the Operator did during an outage. The assistant reads stored modules, effect reports, scaling actions, and admission records as needed to answer. Use slash commands Type / to list available skills. Use the arrow keys to select, Enter to run, Tab to complete, and Esc to dismiss. Disabled skills are omitted. Command Purpose Requires an LLM /help List skills and argument requirements. No /report Produce a 24-hour usage report with document and JSON downloads. No /export Export the last 24 hours of service status. No /tasks List your AI scheduled tasks, next runs, and recent results. No /attention Explain modules needing attention. Yes /outage Review outages, queued reports, and degradation. Yes /actions [module] Explain scaling actions, optionally for a module. Yes /effect <module> Explain a module's forecasting effectiveness. Yes; module required /admission Explain admission records. Yes Reports and exports are built directly from stored facts and work without an LLM connection. The global switch and access permissions still apply. Manage and write skills Use AI configuration → Skill management. Built-in skills can be enabled or disabled; their prompts are read-only and they cannot be deleted. Model-dependent skills can select an LLM; otherwise they use the default. Custom skills define a command, title, description, argument mode (none, required, or optional), model, and prompt. Reference the argument using {{args}} . For example, create /review with a required module argument: Text Copy Analyze the last 24 hours of forecasts and scaling actions for module {{args}}. Separate recorded facts, possible causes, and missing information. Save and enable the skill to make it available in chat. Its selected model must be available; a skill without one follows the default connection. Data scope and actions The assistant queries existing records and does not change algorithm parameters, workload resources, or replicas. Forecasting remains with the forecasting methods, and execution remains with platform rules and the Operator. Read explanations alongside their underlying records. Chat can create, list, and delete the user's own AI scheduled tasks . These query the platform and send answers without resource changes. Tasks created through chat send only to the current user's own email. Chat, skills, and exports use assistant:chat . LLM, skill, and task management have separate permissions. Assistant access currently exposes platform-wide data, rather than an owner-only subset of modules. Troubleshooting Missing entry: check the global switch and chat permission. Reports work but questions fail: check the enabled default LLM, endpoint, model name, tool-calling compatibility, and credentials. Missing skill: check activation and supply required arguments. Incomplete answer: confirm that collection, recommendations, and execution records exist for the requested window.

title: LLM configuration
summary: Configure default and selected models, tools, advanced settings, and credentials.
text: Add a language model connection In AI configuration → LLM management, add a name, provider type, API base URL, model identifier, and credential. Test connection checks the current form. Include the provider's base prefix, such as /v1 , rather than a complete chat endpoint path. The current provider type uses the OpenAI-compatible protocol. Compatible gateways and self-hosted services can be configured; native Anthropic and Gemini protocols are not current provider types. Choose a model supporting tool calls to query platform data. Enabled, default, and selected models Multiple connections may be enabled. Ordinary questions, skills, and tasks without a selected model use the default connection; without an explicit default, the earliest enabled connection is used. A default connection must be enabled. Skills and tasks may select their own model. LLM management is for language models. Model management under forecasting connects time-series models such as Chronos for numerical forecasts; the two connection types are managed separately. Advanced settings Setting Purpose Request timeout Default 90 seconds, range 5–600, for one model request. Tool rounds Default 6, range 1–12, limiting successive tool-call rounds for a question. Temperature Optional sampling setting, subject to provider support. Maximum tokens Bounds a reply; zero omits the limit and lets the service decide. Context length Context budget; older messages are trimmed first. Zero means unknown and disables trimming by this setting. Proxy and TLS Configure a proxy or per-connection certificate-verification bypass. Retain verification for normal certificate connections. Custom headers Additional gateway headers, stored encrypted without returning saved plaintext. Custom JSON parameters Additional service parameters; model, messages, tools, stream, and other platform-managed fields cannot be overridden. Test connection uses the current endpoint, model, and advanced settings. Editing can reuse an existing credential. Save after testing and review the default selection. Credentials and permissions Credentials and custom header values are encrypted and are not returned in plaintext in lists or edit forms. Connection management and chat have separate permissions. System settings retain only the global assistant.enabled switch. Manage endpoints, credentials, and limits in LLM management. Explicit database migration moves legacy assistant parameters into connection records. After connecting Test the connection and verify the model identifier and credential. Enable it, select the default, and ask the assistant a question requiring platform data. Review tool reads and the answer to verify tool-call compatibility. Select other enabled models for skills or tasks with different needs.

title: AI scheduled tasks and email
summary: Ask on a schedule, retain answers, and deliver them by email.
text: Ask on a schedule and email the answer An AI scheduled task combines a prompt, schedule, recipients, answer language, and optional LLM. The platform asks the model at the scheduled time using the assistant's platform-query tools, stores the answer, and sends it by email. Examples include daily status summaries, weekly effectiveness reviews, and periodic degradation checks. Tasks do not modify resources or parameters. Results depend on the prompt, available records, and model. Scheduled questions do not replace continuous alert rules. Create a task Ask in chat: “Every Monday at 9, email me the usage status of all modules.” The assistant reports the schedule and next run. The current user must have an identity and valid email; chat-created tasks send only to that user's own address, regardless of other recipients in the prompt. Use /tasks to list your tasks. Administrators manage all tasks under AI configuration → Scheduled tasks, including prompts, schedules, recipients, language, activation, and models. They can run a task immediately and inspect each answer. Schedules and timezones Schedules use the platform timezone, UTC+8 by default. The examples below assume UTC+8. The minimum interval is one hour, each user may have 20 tasks, and prompts are limited to 2000 characters. Schedule Meaning 0 9 * * 1 Every Monday at 09:00. 0 8 * * * Every day at 08:00. 0 9 1 * * The first day of each month at 09:00. @every 24h A 24-hour interval, rather than a fixed daily clock time. Check the displayed next run before saving. Missed historical slots are not replayed individually: an overdue task runs once after recovery, then advances to a future slot. A task still running skips the next occurrence to avoid overlap. Configure email Configure SMTP in System management → System parameters, under notifications. Tasks send through the platform notification channel. Parameter Purpose notify.email.host / port SMTP server and port. notify.email.security starttls , tls , or none , matching the server. notify.email.username / password Login credentials; passwords are encrypted and masked. notify.email.from Sender address. notify.email.skip_verify Whether to bypass server certificate verification. notify.email.timeout_seconds Connection and delivery timeout. Password authentication is sent only over encrypted or local connections. When the answer of a task is HTML (ask the model for an HTML mail in the prompt) the mail carries an HTML and a plain-text version; otherwise it is plain text with Markdown retained as text. For how to fill in the mail server, the encryption and the usual errors see Email (SMTP) setup . Runs and retries Runs use the task center. Inspect answers, tools read, recipients, and delivery status. Retries reuse an existing answer rather than asking again, and recipients already sent successfully are not resent on a retry of the same job. For missing mail, check activation and next run, the selected or default model, task-center errors, SMTP, and recipient addresses. Configure missing models or email channels before retrying.

title: Dashboard and activity
summary: Review module status, attention flags, and applied scaling activity.
text: Review platform activity on the home page Users with home-page access land on the dashboard after login. A shared time window shows enabled and total modules, operating modes, modules needing attention, applied scaling actions, and failed runs. Modules needing attention Flag What to inspect Repeated failure At least three consecutive failures: inspect recent errors, sources, and model runs. Degraded recommendation Review sources and fallback reasons. Expired recommendation Check scheduling, forecasting, and decision refresh. No recommendation A module expected to produce advice has not done so; review module and metric settings. Bypass Confirm whether manual intervention is intentional. Observe-only modules and modules with prediction disabled are not flagged solely for missing advice. Bypass may be intentional; read its reason. Distinguish execution and effectiveness The dashboard reads existing state without starting forecasts, execution, or repairs. The scaling chart aggregates successfully applied Operator actions over time, not forecast recommendations. Empty periods show zero actions. Open Effect report from an attention row to inspect accuracy, timeliness, capacity, and stability.

title: Monitoring and troubleshooting
summary: Trace issues from data sources and model runs to actual replica readiness.
text: Troubleshoot along the workflow Symptom Check first No history Source, template variables, labels, time range, and units. Some models have no results Sample requirements, parameters, inputs, and runtime in model-run details. Evaluation is empty Whether target times have arrived and actuals have been collected. Fallback advice Snapshot sources, input freshness, eligibility, and recovery state. Replicas are unchanged Authorization, bypass, conflicts, expiry, step limits, and cooldowns. Desired count changed but capacity is low Current replicas, Ready status, Pod startup, and preparation time. Inspect metrics and curves Use the metric catalog and query tools to compare history, forecasts, actual performance, freshness, and runtime status. Distinguish missing samples from observations; connections across gaps are not measurements. External monitoring Set metrics.listen to expose /metrics , /healthz , and /readyz . Platform metrics use kube_res_foresight_* ; Operator metrics use kube_res_foresight_operator_* . Metrics observe the workflow rather than replacing snapshots, action reports, or readiness. Synchronous admission does not wait for long Prometheus queries or inference. Review connected records Follow a module through model runs, forecasts, evaluations, recommendations, admission, and scaling. For offline review, use audit exports with the appropriate scope and permissions. Watch decision sources and scaling delays Distinguish platform responses, cached decisions, recovery, and expired caches. Inspect kube_res_foresight_operator_decision_source_total and kube_res_foresight_operator_decision_cache_age_seconds , then correlate expansion timeliness with Ready-replica curves to separate forecast lag from slow capacity readiness. No model output is expected when prediction is disabled. Check the module's prediction mode before investigating data, models, and execution.

title: Administration
summary: Manage access, scheduled tasks, audit, and time settings.
text: Users, roles, and permissions Use user, role, menu, and API permissions to define access. Separate viewing results, editing policies, and authorizing execution. Grant machine credentials minimal permissions for their purpose. Directory authentication Configure LDAP under System → System parameters: connection, user and group queries, role mapping, checks, and synchronization. LDAPS / StartTLS settings are supported. Local accounts keep local authentication for emergency access. Parameters, role mapping, and troubleshooting are in LDAP sign-in . Tasks and global settings The task center manages schedules and execution records. Review inputs and errors before retrying. Global settings hold safety gates, look-ahead controls, and defaults; modules hold workload-specific policies and bounds. Storage and display time Store timestamps in UTC. The platform defaults to UTC+8, configurable through KUBE_RES_FORESIGHT_TIMEZONE for logs, database sessions, and new module schedules. Pages display UTC+8 regardless of browser timezone. Schedule intervals use explicit IANA timezones. Logs, retention, and export Login logs record authentication; operation logs track configuration and exports. Recommendation, execution, admission, and degradation records explain resource changes. Set retention for review needs and back up both the database and stable encryption key. Control history and admission record volume Set forecast.history_retention_days to override history retention; the default 0 keeps each record type's built-in period. forecast.evaluation_max_per_module keeps the latest 20,000 measured evaluations per module by default, with a minimum of 100. Admission calls need request_uid to create records, with deduplication by UID. With revision information, admission records creation and the first Pod of each new revision. Later scaling or replacement Pods are processed normally without individual records. Enable forecast.admission_record_scaling to include them. Calls with a UID but no revision information continue to be recorded individually. AI configuration and notifications assistant.enabled controls the chat entry. AI configuration manages LLM connections , skills , and scheduled tasks . Grant their menu permissions separately from assistant:chat . Email uses notify.email.* under notification settings; see Email (SMTP) setup for how to fill them in. Check the model connection, user email, and SMTP; inspect task results through task records and the task center.

title: LDAP sign-in
summary: Set up directory login, how groups are read, and role mapping, and reuse the LDAP settings other systems already have.
text: How a login is told apart The sign-in page has no source option. The platform decides from the user name and the local database: Case Result The name exists locally and is a local account Only the local password is checked; the directory is not contacted. admin keeps working when the directory is down. The name exists locally and is an LDAP account The password is checked against the directory only. The name is unknown and LDAP is enabled The directory authenticates. On success the roles come from the role mappings and the LDAP user is created. The name is unknown and LDAP is disabled The login fails. A directory user with the same name as a local account never takes it over. An LDAP user's local password is random and unusable, and the password cannot be changed in the user center; change it in the directory. The user list and the user center show the account source. Parameters Set them one by one under System → System parameters, in the LDAP category. Each is saved on its own. Parameter Meaning ldap.url Directory address, such as ldaps://ldap.example.com:636 . ldap:// requires StartTLS. ldap.start_tls / ldap.skip_verify StartTLS; whether to skip certificate verification. Do not skip it when you can provide the CA. ldap.ca_cert CA (PEM) for a self-signed certificate. Shown masked after saving. ldap.bind_dn / ldap.bind_password Service account used to look users up. The password is stored encrypted; set the bind DN first. ldap.user_base_dn Where the user search starts, such as dc=example,dc=com . ldap.user_filter Filter that finds the user. It must contain exactly one %s (the login name), for example (cn=%s) or (&(objectClass=person)(uid=%s)) . ldap.display_name_attr / email_attr / phone_attr Attributes for display name, email and phone, refreshed at each login. ldap.member_of_attr Attribute of the user entry that lists the DNs of its groups, usually memberOf . When set, the groups are read from it. ldap.group_base_dn / ldap.group_filter Without memberOf, look the user up in the group entries: in the filter %s is the user DN and %u the login name, such as (member=%s) . Both are set or both are empty: setting one while the other is empty fills in a usual value, and clearing one clears both. ldap.group_name_attr Attribute of a group entry used as its name, cn by default. ldap.group_role_mappings Group-to-role mappings, below. ldap.default_role_code Role of users in no mapped group. Empty means those users cannot sign in. ldap.timeout_seconds Connection and query timeout, 1 to 120 seconds. ldap.enabled Whether directory login is on. Enabling validates the whole configuration and connects to the directory once. If that fails, LDAP is not enabled and the reason is shown, so set ldap.enabled last. Two ways to get the groups Use either, or both: the results are merged. Read memberOf of the user : set ldap.member_of_attr ; no group base DN or filter is needed. Each value (a group DN) matches either as the full DN or as the value of its first RDN ( cn=ops,ou=groups,… matches ops ). Search the group entries : set ldap.group_base_dn and ldap.group_filter , and take the name from ldap.group_name_attr . Usual filters: (member=%s) for OpenLDAP groupOfNames, (memberUid=%u) for posixGroup, and (member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=%s) for AD when nested groups count. Role mapping ldap.group_role_mappings takes one group=role code per line: ops=ADMIN dev=VIEWER ou=sre,ou=platform,dc=example,dc=com=ADMIN The left side is a group name ( cn ) or a full DN, case-insensitive; spaces inside a full DN must match what the directory returns. The right side is the role code , listed under Authorization → Roles. The role must exist and be enabled. The line is split at the last = , so full DNs work as they are. A group may appear on several lines to grant several roles; a user in several groups gets the union. Lines starting with # are comments and blank lines are ignored. A malformed or repeated line is rejected on save. A user in no mapped group gets ldap.default_role_code ; with neither, the login is refused. An existing LDAP user who loses every role is disabled and their sessions end. Reusing an existing LDAP configuration Other systems in your company (a wiki, a code host, monitoring, CI) usually use the same directory, and their LDAP settings already hold what is needed here. Copy each value to its parameter: What you already have Where it goes Server address, port, SSL on or off ldap.url ; with SSL write ldaps://address:port StartTLS, skipping certificate verification ldap.start_tls , ldap.skip_verify The lookup account (bind DN) and its password ldap.bind_dn , ldap.bind_password Where users are searched (base DN) ldap.user_base_dn The user search filter and its placeholder for the login name ldap.user_filter , with the placeholder written as %s . (cn=${username}) , (uid={0}) and (sAMAccountName=%(user)s) all become a form like (cn=%s) Attribute names for the name and the email ldap.display_name_attr , ldap.email_attr The attribute of the user entry that lists its groups (often memberOf) ldap.member_of_attr Where groups are searched and the membership filter (without memberOf) ldap.group_base_dn , ldap.group_filter The table of group DN to role or permission ldap.group_role_mappings , one group DN=role code of this platform per line Roles in the other system (administrator, editor, read-only) have no fixed counterpart here: use the role codes you created under Authorization → Roles. The built-in administrator role is ADMIN and has every permission, so check before granting it to a whole group. Complete configuration examples and what happens in one sign-in Two common directories follow, with what each parameter holds and what the platform does in one sign-in, side by side. Addresses, DNs and group names are examples; replace them with the values of your directory. Example 1: OpenLDAP, groups from the membership in group entries The directory holds: LDIF Copy dn: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com uid: alice cn: Alice Zhang mail: alice@example.com dn: cn=sre,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com objectClass: groupOfNames cn: sre member: uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com Set the system parameters like this (System → System parameters → LDAP; each item is saved on its own, enable last): Parameter Value Note ldap.url ldaps://ldap.example.com:636 LDAPS; with ldap:// StartTLS must be on. ldap.bind_dn cn=readonly,dc=example,dc=com A read-only service account used to search for users. ldap.bind_password the password of the service account Stored encrypted. ldap.user_base_dn ou=people,dc=example,dc=com Users are searched below it. ldap.user_filter (uid=%s) %s becomes the login name. ldap.display_name_attr cn The display name. ldap.email_attr mail The email. ldap.group_base_dn ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com Group entries are searched here. ldap.group_filter (member=%s) Here %s is the DN of the user , not the login name. ldap.group_name_attr cn (default) The attribute of a group entry that is the group name. ldap.group_role_mappings sre=ADMIN dev=VIEWER One group=role code per line. ldap.default_role_code empty Someone in no mapped group cannot sign in. To let them in read-only, give the code of a read-only role. ldap.enabled true Set last: enabling checks the whole configuration and connects to the directory once. What happens when alice signs in: The platform connects to the directory over LDAPS and signs in with the service account cn=readonly,… . It searches below ou=people,… with (uid=alice) . It finds one entry uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com ; none is "user not found", more than one is refused (the filter must match exactly one person). Special characters in the typed login name are escaped and cannot rewrite the filter. It signs in once more with that DN and the password alice typed. The password is checked only by the directory ; the platform neither stores nor compares it. It reads cn and mail : the display name Alice Zhang and the email. Groups: it searches below ou=groups,… with (member=uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com) and finds the group cn=sre , group name sre . By the mapping sre=ADMIN alice gets the ADMIN role; the local database has no alice, so a user whose source is LDAP is created and signed in. Example 2: Active Directory, reading memberOf directly Parameter Value ldap.url ldaps://ad.example.com:636 ldap.bind_dn CN=svc-krf,OU=Service Accounts,DC=example,DC=com ldap.user_base_dn DC=example,DC=com ldap.user_filter (&(objectClass=user)(sAMAccountName=%s)) ldap.display_name_attr / ldap.email_attr displayName / mail ldap.member_of_attr memberOf ldap.group_base_dn / ldap.group_filter empty (not needed with memberOf) ldap.group_role_mappings Platform-Admins=ADMIN CN=Platform-Readers,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=com=VIEWER The memberOf of an AD user entry holds the full DN of each group, for example CN=Platform-Admins,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=com . The left side of a mapping may be the full DN or just the value of its first segment ( Platform-Admins ); the platform matches both. The second line shows the full-DN form: the line is split at the last = , so the whole DN in front is untouched. To count nested groups too, do not use memberOf but the group filter (member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=%s) . Check before enabling The service account finds the user: sign in with it in any LDAP client and search user_base_dn for a known user with the same filter; it should return exactly one entry. The role code exists and is enabled: the code on the right of a mapping must match the one under Authorization → Roles. Try an ordinary user, then an administrator: make sure a mapped role does not give a whole group more than it should. Synchronization and disabling Users who were deleted or disabled in the directory, or who no longer belong to a mapped group, are disabled by the synchronization and lose their sessions; users the directory enabled again are restored, except those an administrator disabled. When the directory cannot be reached no account is changed, so an outage does not lock everyone out. Troubleshooting Symptom Check Cannot enable; the directory check failed Address and port, the certificate (a self-signed one needs the CA or, for now, skipped verification), the service account and password, and the network. Sign-in fails and the page only says invalid credentials Read ldap login refused in the platform log; its reason says why. the user belongs to no group mapped to a role Authentication passed but no role resulted. groups found in the parentheses is what the directory returned: empty means the way of getting groups or the filter is wrong; with names, add a mapping or set a default role. a local account with this name exists A local account has the name and the directory never takes it over. Use the local password, or let an administrator deal with the account. One setting is refused on save While enabled, every change validates the whole configuration. The address, user base DN and user filter cannot be empty, and the bind DN and password go together. Local accounts always sign in with their local password; the directory being down does not affect them.

title: Email (SMTP) setup
summary: Set the mail server, the encryption and the sender, fill it in for common mail services, send a test mail first and read the errors.
text: What the email channel is and who uses it The email channel lets the platform send mail to given addresses through an SMTP server. What uses it today is the AI scheduled tasks : a task has a model answer on a schedule and mails the answer to its recipients. The channel only hands a message to an SMTP server and knows nothing about the content; when it is not set up, a task run fails and the task center says why, so no mail is lost silently. All of it is set in the Notify category of "System → System parameters"; there is no configuration file. Each item is saved on its own, and a parameter just saved takes effect within 10 seconds. Once it is set, the "Send test mail" button on the same page is the quickest check. Parameters Parameter Default Meaning notify.email.host empty The host name or IP of the SMTP server. Empty means the channel is not set up and sending fails at once. notify.email.port 587 The port, 1 to 65535. Usual pairs: 587 + starttls , 465 + tls , 25 + none . notify.email.security starttls How the connection is encrypted: starttls (connect in clear, then upgrade to encryption), tls (the whole connection is TLS from the start, also called implicit TLS / SMTPS) or none (no encryption). notify.email.username empty The account that signs in to the SMTP server. Leave empty when the server needs no sign-in. notify.email.password empty The password or app password of the account. Stored encrypted and shown as a mask; sending the mask back keeps the stored value. notify.email.from empty The sender address, required. It may be reports@example.com or with a display name, "kube-res-foresight <reports@example.com>" . A mail service usually requires it to be the sign-in account or an address that account may send as. notify.email.skip_verify false Whether to skip checking the server certificate. Turn it on, for a while, only for a server with a self-signed certificate; with it on the connection can be impersonated, so do not use it when a trusted certificate is available. notify.email.timeout_seconds 30 The time one mail may take from connecting and signing in to being handed to the server, 5 to 300 seconds. There is no separate "enable" switch: when host , port and from are valid the channel is usable. Encryption and the password: when the sign-in password is sent The platform uses the standard SMTP PLAIN sign-in. For safety, the account password is sent only over an encrypted connection , or to a server on this machine; on an unencrypted connection to another host the sign-in is refused instead of sending the password in clear. security Usual port Process Account and password? starttls 587 Connect in clear and greet; the server must announce STARTTLS; then upgrade to TLS, sign in and send. When the server does not support it, it is an error, not a fall back to clear text. Yes (after the upgrade) tls 465 TLS from the first byte, then sign in and send. Yes none 25 No encryption at all. Only when the server is on this machine; for an internal relay without authentication. How to fill it in for common mail services The host names, addresses and passwords below are examples; replace them with your own. Follow the instructions of your mail provider for the details (some need an "app password" or SMTP sign-in allowed in an admin console). A company mailbox / Microsoft 365 style 587 + STARTTLS Parameter Value notify.email.host smtp.example.com notify.email.port 587 notify.email.security starttls notify.email.username reports@example.com notify.email.password the password or app password of that account notify.email.from kube-res-foresight <reports@example.com> 465 + implicit TLS The same as the table above, only port becomes 465 and security becomes tls . An internal relay, no sign-in Parameter Value notify.email.host mail-relay.internal notify.email.port 25 notify.email.security none notify.email.username / password empty notify.email.from reports@example.com (a sender the relay allows) With this setup the content of the mail travels in clear text inside the network; use it only on a trusted network. An internal server with a self-signed certificate Fill in the port and the encryption the server really uses, then set notify.email.skip_verify to true . This is a stopgap: the certificate is not checked and the connection can be impersonated; for long-term use give the server a trusted certificate. What the mail looks like The content is UTF-8 in base64, so a Chinese subject displays properly. When the answer of a task is HTML, the mail carries a plain-text and an HTML version (multipart/alternative): a client that supports HTML shows the version with headings, tables and colours, any other shows the plain text. The platform removes scripts, frames and objects from the HTML, which mail clients do not show anyway. Line breaks in the content are never used to build a mail header. One mail goes to one recipient; a task with several recipients sends to each on its own, and one failing does not make a recipient that was served get it again. Send a test mail first In "System → System parameters" the Notify category has "Send test mail": enter an address and the platform sends a test message with the parameters as saved now. On success it says sent; on failure it shows the words of the mail server, the most useful thing for troubleshooting. A parameter just changed takes effect within 10 seconds, so wait a moment before testing. Troubleshooting Message (excerpt) Cause and what to check the e-mail channel is not set up: the SMTP host (notify.email.host) is empty The host is not set. the SMTP port (notify.email.port) is not valid The port is not between 1 and 65535. the sender address (notify.email.from) is not set / is not valid The sender is empty or malformed; with a display name write Name <address> . the security (notify.email.security) is starttls, tls or none security must be one of these three values. could not reach the SMTP server host:port Cannot connect: the host name, the port, a firewall or an egress network policy. In a container check that the Pod of the platform can reach the address. the SMTP server did not greet Connected but the server did not greet in SMTP; usually the port and the encryption do not match, for example starttls on 465, which should be tls . the SMTP server does not offer STARTTLS The server cannot upgrade to encryption: use the way it supports ( tls ), or none only when it is an unencrypted internal relay. STARTTLS failed / certificate errors The certificate is not trusted or the name does not match. Check the certificate of the server; a self-signed one may be allowed for a while with skip_verify . the SMTP server refused the sign-in The account or the password is wrong, or the server requires an app password or has not allowed SMTP sign-in for that account. the SMTP server refused the sender The sender is not allowed: usually it has to be the sign-in account or an address that account may send as. the SMTP server refused the recipient … The recipient was refused: a wrong address, or the server does not allow sending to external domains (a relay restriction). When a task run fails the error also appears in the run record of the task center, and a recipient that was already served does not get the mail again on a retry.

title: Common questions
summary: Find answers about setup, model choice, operating modes, and resource updates.
text: Can this website manage my cluster? This website provides project information and guides. Deploy the management platform separately to connect sources, configure modules, inspect advice, and authorize actions. Which model should I choose? Start with a baseline and compare resource error, peak underestimation, and runtime over the same history and horizon. Complexity does not replace workload performance. Available forecasts can also contribute to consensus. Can I use HPA or KEDA at the same time? They may manage other workloads, but must not control the same target replicas. Stop the old controller and release ownership before switching. Why are predictions or scores missing? First check whether prediction is enabled and whether No prediction is selected. New modules start with prediction disabled; configured fallback defaults are intentional. Then check sources, template labels, units, history, model runs, and freshness. Actual scores require the target time to arrive and matching observations to be collected. Do running Pods immediately receive updated advice? Admission affects new Pods; running configurations change through creation or rolling updates. Replica scaling is a separate action performed by the Operator. How do I pause automation? Enable module bypass or disable the corresponding global gate, then return to Observe or Recommend. Review actual resources before restoring earlier settings; bypass does not undo previous changes.
